creator: Alexander Terp
description:
Finding out that an agent has finished means polling `muster window --json`; nothing in the CLI waits for a state change, and nothing says when a pane's state last changed.

Measured 2026-09-04: one session integrated the work of nine agents, each in its own pane. Its loop ran `muster window --json` every 180 seconds, filtered the nine pane names with jq, and diffed the states against the previous tick. It ran about two hours, some forty snapshots, and caught every finish. It is still the wrong shape in two ways.

A finished worker waited up to three minutes before anybody knew. Nine workers finishing on their own clocks made that a real cost: every rebase, gate run and next brief started late. Shortening the interval buys that back with more round trips, and each snapshot here was an ssh hop, because the caller sat on the devenv (a_29e9be7aQ).

A snapshot also cannot say how long a pane has been in its state. `working` at one tick and `working` at the next reads as one long turn, and reads the same if the agent finished and was handed new work in between. Nothing in `panes[]` says when the state last changed.

Muster already holds the transitions: the sidebar repaints on them, and a_28XbMv3tn made sure none is lost before its watcher connects. The caller re-derives them from snapshots only because the CLI offers nothing else.

Done when a caller can block on a state change instead of polling - `muster pane wait --pane P --until idle --timeout 600`, or `muster window --watch` printing one line per transition across every pane, JSON included - and `window --json` says how long each pane has been in its state. Which shape, and whether the daemon's per-pane subscription (a_27N6pklkl) is what sits underneath, is for whoever picks this up.
title: ⏳ Nothing waits for an agent's state to change, so a caller polls window --json
